title: Famotidine: Acid Suppression With Renal Awareness
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Famotidine reduces gastric acid through H2-receptor blockade. In older adults and patients with renal impairment, dose accumulation can increase adverse CNS effects, so renal context matters even for a familiar acid-suppressing drug.
recognize: Confusion or new CNS symptoms in a frail or renally impaired patient may be medication-related.
Persistent GI bleeding symptoms are not explained away by acid suppression.
priorities: Review indication, renal function, and symptom pattern.
Escalate hematemesis, melena with instability, severe abdominal pain, or new marked confusion.
assessMonitor: Trend symptom relief, renal function, mental status, bleeding signs, and need for continued therapy.
interventions: Administer as ordered and reinforce avoidance of unnecessary duplicate OTC acid suppressants.
medicationSafety: Renal dose adjustment may be required.
Do not let symptom relief delay evaluation of alarm features such as bleeding, progressive dysphagia, or weight loss.
teaching: Report GI bleeding, progressive swallowing difficulty, or persistent symptoms despite treatment.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; alarm symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating new confusion in severe renal impairment as normal aging while continuing the same famotidine regimen.
oneLinePearl: Famotidine is familiar, but kidney function still matters.

title: Sucralfate: Coat the Ulcer, Separate the Medications
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over ulcerated mucosa. Its major nursing issue is timing because it can interfere with absorption of other oral drugs, and aluminum exposure matters in significant renal impairment.
recognize: Constipation is common.
A crowded medication schedule raises interaction risk because several drugs may need separation from sucralfate.
priorities: Review the entire oral-medication schedule before administration.
Assess bowel pattern and renal context.
assessMonitor: Trend symptom improvement, constipation, adherence, medication spacing, and renal function when clinically relevant.
interventions: Give according to the prescribed empty-stomach schedule and separate interacting medications as directed.
medicationSafety: Sucralfate can reduce absorption of selected medications.
Aluminum accumulation is a concern in advanced renal dysfunction.
teaching: Follow the timing plan rather than taking all medications together.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; medication-interaction reconciliation requires licensed clinical review.
examTrap: Giving sucralfate at the same time as every other oral medication for convenience.
oneLinePearl: Sucralfate protects the stomach but can block other pills.

title: Mesalamine: Anti-Inflammatory Therapy With Kidney Monitoring
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Mesalamine treats inflammatory bowel disease through local anti-inflammatory activity. Renal injury, acute intolerance reactions, and formulation-specific administration are key safety points.
recognize: Worsening cramping, bloody diarrhea, fever, headache, or rash soon after starting can resemble an IBD flare but may represent acute mesalamine intolerance.
Renal impairment can develop during treatment.
priorities: Review renal function and baseline symptom pattern.
Escalate sudden worsening that may represent intolerance rather than automatically increasing therapy.
assessMonitor: Trend renal function, stool frequency/blood, abdominal pain, hydration, and rash/fever.
interventions: Administer the exact delayed-release/extended-release formulation as directed; do not assume all products are interchangeable.
medicationSafety: Renal monitoring is required.
Some products should not be crushed or chewed because delivery location matters.
redFlags: Severe bloody diarrhea with fever after initiation
teaching: Report sudden worsening of colitis-like symptoms after starting the drug and keep renal monitoring appointments.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; suspected intolerance or renal injury requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Assuming every increase in bloody diarrhea is simply an IBD flare after mesalamine is started.
oneLinePearl: Mesalamine treats the bowel—still monitor the kidneys.

title: Pancrelipase: Enzymes Must Meet the Meal
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Pancrelipase replaces pancreatic enzymes and works only when taken with meals or snacks. Product strength, timing, swallowing instructions, nutrition response, and excessive-dose complications matter.
recognize: Persistent greasy stools, weight loss, bloating, or poor growth can signal inadequate enzyme delivery or dosing.
High exposure has been associated with fibrosing colonopathy, especially in cystic fibrosis.
priorities: Give with food and verify the exact product/strength.
Monitor stool quality, weight/nutrition, and GI symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, stool characteristics, abdominal symptoms, nutritional status, and adherence with every meal/snack.
interventions: Follow product-specific instructions for patients who cannot swallow capsules; do not crush enteric-coated microspheres.
medicationSafety: Pancrelipase products are not automatically interchangeable unit-for-unit.
Do not chew enteric-coated particles because oral mucosal irritation and loss of enzyme protection can occur.
teaching: Take enzymes with every meal and snack—not hours later.
delegationScope: Routine administration and meal coordination may be within scope; persistent malabsorption requires licensed clinical follow-up.
examTrap: Giving pancrelipase two hours after the meal because it was missed at mealtime.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatic enzymes work when enzymes and food arrive together.

title: Loperamide: Slow Diarrhea Only When Slowing Is Safe
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Loperamide reduces intestinal motility, which can help uncomplicated diarrhea but can be harmful when the bowel needs to clear an invasive infection or when ileus/toxic megacolon is developing.
recognize: Bloody stool, high fever, severe abdominal distention, or significant tenderness argues against reflexive antimotility treatment.
Excessive doses can cause serious cardiac toxicity.
priorities: Assess cause clues, hydration, blood in stool, fever, abdominal distention, and bowel sounds before giving.
Escalate suspected C. difficile, dysentery, ileus, toxic megacolon, or severe dehydration.
assessMonitor: Trend stool frequency, hydration, abdominal exam, fever, electrolytes when indicated, and medication use.
interventions: Prioritize hydration and cause-directed treatment when needed rather than simply suppressing stool output.
medicationSafety: Do not exceed recommended dosing; high-dose misuse has caused dangerous dysrhythmias.
Avoid routine use when bloody inflammatory diarrhea or toxic megacolon is suspected unless specifically directed.
teaching: Seek care for bloody stool, high fever, severe pain, dehydration, or persistent diarrhea rather than repeatedly increasing OTC doses.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope after assessment criteria are established; red-flag diarrhea requires licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Giving loperamide for severe bloody diarrhea with fever before evaluating for invasive infection.
oneLinePearl: Do not slow a gut that may need to clear infection.

title: Polyethylene Glycol 3350: Osmotic Laxative, Not an Obstruction Fix
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Polyethylene glycol retains water in the stool and is useful for constipation, but severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or obstruction symptoms require evaluation rather than more laxative.
recognize: Bloating, loose stools, or cramping may occur.
No stool with progressive distention and vomiting suggests a problem beyond routine constipation.
priorities: Assess bowel history, hydration, abdominal symptoms, and obstruction red flags.
Hold/escalate for suspected obstruction or acute abdomen.
assessMonitor: Trend bowel frequency/consistency, hydration, abdominal distention, and response to therapy.
interventions: Mix the powder according to product directions and support adequate fluid intake when not restricted.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate laxatives blindly in suspected obstruction.
Chronic or unexplained constipation deserves evaluation rather than indefinite self-treatment.
teaching: Use as directed and report persistent constipation or obstruction symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine bowel-regimen administration may be within scope; acute abdominal red flags require licensed assessment.
examTrap: Giving another osmotic laxative dose to a patient with vomiting, severe distention, and no flatus.
oneLinePearl: PEG softens stool; it does not push through an obstruction.

title: Bisacodyl: Stimulate the Bowel, Protect the Enteric Coat
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Bisacodyl is a stimulant laxative for short-term constipation relief. Enteric-coated tablets should not be crushed or chewed and should not be taken close to milk or antacids because premature coating dissolution can increase irritation.
recognize: Cramping and abdominal discomfort can occur.
Rectal bleeding or failure to have a bowel movement after use can signal a more serious condition.
priorities: Assess for abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, sudden bowel-habit change, or obstruction concerns before routine use.
Protect the enteric coating and timing instructions.
assessMonitor: Trend bowel response, abdominal symptoms, rectal bleeding, and duration/frequency of laxative use.
interventions: Give delayed-release tablets whole with water and follow current product timing guidance.
medicationSafety: Current 2026 OTC labeling advises not to crush/chew and not to take within one hour of milk or an antacid.
Repeated use beyond short-term directions requires clinical review.
redFlags: No bowel movement after use with worsening symptoms
teaching: Use for occasional constipation and seek evaluation if ongoing laxatives are repeatedly needed.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope after bowel assessment parameters are established.
examTrap: Crushing an enteric-coated bisacodyl tablet into applesauce for easier swallowing.
oneLinePearl: Bisacodyl stimulates the bowel—keep the enteric coat intact.

title: Prochlorperazine: Antiemetic With Movement-Disorder Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Prochlorperazine can control severe nausea/vomiting but dopamine blockade can cause dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, hypotension, and rare neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
recognize: Neck spasm, oculogyric crisis, jaw tightness, severe restlessness, rigidity, fever, or autonomic instability are medication-safety clues.
Older adults are more vulnerable to sedation, falls, and movement effects.
priorities: Assess mental status, BP, gait/fall risk, and abnormal movements.
Escalate acute dystonia, NMS features, or severe hypotension immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend nausea control, sedation, BP, movement symptoms, hydration, and temperature when toxicity is suspected.
interventions: Use fall precautions and administer ordered rescue treatment for acute dystonia when indicated.
medicationSafety: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine, not a benign antiemetic.
Avoid additive CNS-depressant exposure when possible and monitor closely when unavoidable.
teaching: Report involuntary movements, severe restlessness, neck/jaw spasm, or fever with rigidity.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; abnormal movement or NMS assessment requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Treating new neck spasm after prochlorperazine as anxiety.
oneLinePearl: An antiemetic that blocks dopamine can create movement emergencies.

title: Promethazine: Sedation, Pediatric Respiratory Risk, and Tissue Injury
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Promethazine is sedating and injectable formulations can cause catastrophic tissue injury. It is contraindicated in children younger than 2 years because of potentially fatal respiratory depression, and parenteral administration demands route/site vigilance.
recognize: Excess sedation, slowed breathing, burning, severe pain, swelling, blanching, or neurovascular change at an injection site are urgent safety cues.
Concurrent opioids or other CNS depressants increase respiratory-depression risk.
priorities: Verify age, route, formulation, respiratory status, and CNS-depressant exposure.
Escalate respiratory depression or any evidence of parenteral tissue injury immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory rate, oxygenation, sedation, BP, injection-site perfusion/pain, and fall risk.
interventions: Use the safest ordered route and current product-specific administration precautions.
Stop administration and activate extravasation/tissue-injury response when indicated.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. injection labeling warns of fatal respiratory depression in children under 2 and severe tissue injury including gangrene.
Never use an intra-arterial route.
teaching: Avoid alcohol and unapproved sedating medications; report severe injection-site burning or pain immediately.
delegationScope: Parenteral promethazine authority and route competency vary by facility/state; respiratory or tissue injury requires immediate licensed response.
examTrap: Ignoring intense IV-site burning because promethazine commonly stings.
oneLinePearl: Promethazine can sedate the patient and injure the vein—watch breathing and tissue.
sourceBasis: DailyMed promethazine hydrochloride injection labeling current 2026

title: Scopolamine Patch: Anticholinergic Safety Behind the Ear
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological Therapies
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Transdermal scopolamine prevents motion-related nausea through anticholinergic effects. Dry mouth and blurred vision are common, but confusion, urinary retention, glaucoma symptoms, and accidental eye exposure matter most in vulnerable patients.
recognize: Older adults can develop delirium or urinary retention from anticholinergic burden.
Touching the patch then the eye can dilate the pupil and blur vision.
priorities: Review glaucoma, urinary retention/BPH risk, cognitive status, and other anticholinergic medications.
Wash hands after patch handling and remove old patches before applying a new one.
assessMonitor: Trend mental status, urinary output/retention symptoms, vision/eye pain, dry mouth, and dizziness.
interventions: Apply to clean hairless skin behind the ear according to product directions and document patch location/date.
medicationSafety: Additive anticholinergic effects can worsen delirium, constipation, and urinary retention.
Do not cut transdermal systems unless specifically permitted by the product.
teaching: Wash hands after touching the patch and report severe confusion, urinary retention, or acute eye pain.
delegationScope: Routine patch administration may be within scope; delirium or urinary retention requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Applying a new scopolamine patch without removing the previous patch.
oneLinePearl: Scopolamine is a patch with whole-body anticholinergic effects.
